beats.narration_en: How does a net stop a twenty-ton boulder?
Mountain roads hang steel nets on the slopes above them.
The net is woven from steel rings, like chain mail.
When a rock hits, the net doesn't try to stop it dead.
It stretches like a trampoline, more than twenty feet.
And the ropes that hold it pull through brake rings.
These steel loops shrink and bend, turning the speed into heat.
A slow stop keeps the forces low, so nothing snaps.
The biggest nets stop twenty tons at sixty miles an hour.
Afterward, crews clear the rock and replace the brakes.
That's what those steel nets on mountain cliffs are for.
